reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Ashcraft Pediatric Surgery
clinicalPearls: A neonatal distal small-bowel obstruction caused by abnormally thick, tenacious meconium impacting the terminal ileum
It is the earliest clinical manifestation of cystic fibrosis in a large proportion of affected infants, so all cases warrant sweat testing and CFTR genetic evaluation
Presents in the first days of life with abdominal distension, bilious vomiting, and failure to pass meconium
Abdominal radiographs show dilated small-bowel loops with a soap-bubble or ground-glass appearance in the right lower quadrant and characteristically few air-fluid levels
Divided into simple obstruction and complicated forms with volvulus, atresia, perforation, or meconium peritonitis with calcification
A water-soluble contrast (gastrograffin-type) enema is both diagnostic, showing a microcolon and inspissated pellets, and therapeutic in uncomplicated cases
Surgery is reserved for enemas that fail or for complicated disease, and long-term management addresses the underlying cystic fibrosis
reference.pathophysiology: In meconium ileus, deficient CFTR chloride channel function reduces luminal fluid secretion and, together with abnormal pancreatic enzyme delivery, produces meconium that is dehydrated, viscid, and adherent. This inspissated meconium obstructs the distal ileum, causing proximal small-bowel dilatation and an unused microcolon distally. In complicated disease, the heavy, obstructed loops may twist (volvulus), lose their blood supply, become atretic, or perforate in utero, spilling sterile meconium into the peritoneum and producing meconium peritonitis with dystrophic calcification.
additionalDifferentials: Meconium plug syndrome and small left colon syndrome
Neonatal small left colon in an infant of a diabetic mother
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal radiograph for dilated loops, soap-bubble sign, and any peritoneal calcification suggesting perforation
Water-soluble contrast enema to confirm microcolon and locate inspissated pellets, with therapeutic intent
Sweat chloride testing and CFTR mutation analysis to confirm cystic fibrosis
Serial examination and imaging to detect complicated features such as volvulus or perforation
Prenatal ultrasound review for echogenic bowel, dilated loops, or intra-abdominal calcification
redFlags: Signs of peritonitis, marked tenderness, or abdominal wall erythema indicating perforation or meconium peritonitis
Rapid clinical deterioration or haemodynamic instability suggesting volvulus or ischaemia
Failure of contrast enema to relieve obstruction, mandating operative management
Free intraperitoneal air or a pseudocyst on imaging
reference.prognosis: With prompt relief of obstruction, outcomes for the bowel are generally good, but overall prognosis is dominated by the underlying cystic fibrosis and its pulmonary and pancreatic manifestations. Complicated meconium ileus carries higher perioperative morbidity but survival with modern care remains favourable.
pitfalls: Failing to test for cystic fibrosis in every infant with meconium ileus
Attempting contrast enema treatment when perforation or a complicated lesion is present
Missing an associated atresia or volvulus behind the obstruction
Inadequate attention to hydration status during hyperosmolar contrast enema
Overlooking evolving meconium peritonitis when abdominal calcification is present
